findings.text: VCPU creation hook initializes per-VCPU SEV-ES state. It always initializes a mutex for SNP VMSA handling. For guests without encrypted-state support it succeeds immediately. Otherwise it reserves a dedicated VMSA page using SNP-safe allocation, records both pending and guest VMSA addresses as invalid, and caches whether secure TSC is enabled for the VM.

Decrypted VMSA access is available only to encrypted-state guests. When guest-state protection is not yet active the live VMSA is yielded without allocation or firmware interaction. Debug permission is judged from policy with distinct rules for SNP versus legacy guests. SNP uses a zeroed firmware page plus a SNP debug decrypt request; legacy uses a normal kernel page plus a legacy debug decrypt request. Failure reports absence after releasing scratch resources.

Release of a decrypted VMSA image is a no-op when protection was never active or when the supplied pointer indicates absence. Otherwise the single page holding the image is returned to the page allocator.

A disabled-build fallback provides the same two entry names with degenerate behavior: lookup always reports absence and release performs no action. This preserves call sites when the encrypted-state feature is compiled out.

The VMCB diagnostic dump emits common save fields including system call linkages, paging controls, debug controls, branch trace endpoints and exception trace endpoints. It then branches on encrypted-state guest status. The encrypted branch reports feature flags, shadow stack levels, CET state, extended control state and general registers from the decrypted image. The legacy branch mixes save-area values with cached VCPU register values. An encrypted-state dump always releases its decrypted image on completion.

The encrypted-state save image observed by the dump carries feature flags plus per-privilege shadow stack pointers and user CET state. It also carries the full general register set and extended control registers. The dump treats these fields as authoritative for encrypted guests rather than consulting the host register cache.

For legacy guests the architectural state is split between the VMCB save area and a VCPU register cache. The save area supplies selected values such as stack pointer and accumulator while the cache supplies the remaining general registers including extended registers on 64-bit builds. The dump reflects that split ownership.

Unexpected exit reporting funnels to userspace as an internal error. The run block records an internal-error exit reason with a dedicated unexpected-reason suberror and exactly two payload words: the offending hardware reason and the CPU that performed the last entry.

The internal-error exit uses exit reason KVM_EXIT_INTERNAL_ERROR with suberror KVM_INTERNAL_ERROR_UNEXPECTED_EXIT_REASON and a two-word payload. This shape is part of the userspace contract for unrecognized hardware reasons.

Halt emulation advances past the current instruction and then places the VCPU in the halted multiprocessor state with a halt exit to userspace. The skip and the state transition are combined so that either failure is visible to the caller.
Halted state is represented by multiprocessor state KVM_MP_STATE_HALTED together with exit reason KVM_EXIT_HLT. These values identify a guest halt awaiting userspace or interrupt handling.

Encrypted-state string PIO validates the transfer length from the exit information word. Lengths beyond signed maximum are rejected. Multiplicative overflow of count and element size is rejected. Zero-byte transfers complete successfully without further work. Otherwise a scratch area is prepared and control passes to the generic encrypted PIO path with direction preserved.

The generic encrypted string PIO entry stages the data pointer and remaining count in per-VCPU fields, then dispatches by direction to input or output handling. Size and port travel unchanged to the direction handler.

Encrypted PIO input and output proceed in bounded chunks limited by page capacity divided by element size. Each chunk is offered to kernel PIO emulation and the staged pointer and count advance accordingly. Kernel completion with no remainder reports handled status. A chunk requiring userspace installs a direction-specific completion callback and reports that userspace must run.

PIO progress accounting subtracts the completed element count from the staged remainder and advances the staged data pointer by count times element size. It performs no bounds checking itself; callers guarantee the chunk does not exceed the remainder.

Kernel PIO emulation attempts every element against the PIO bus in order. Success for all elements reports kernel-handled status. If the very first element finds no kernel device, a userspace exit is prepared with port, direction, size and count plus a data window, and kernel handling is declined. Input and output wrappers add tracing around this core behavior.

Userspace PIO uses exit reason KVM_EXIT_IO with direction values KVM_EXIT_IO_IN and KVM_EXIT_IO_OUT. The exit block carries port, size, count and data offset, with the data window located at KVM_PIO_PAGE_OFFSET pages into the shared run area. In-kernel PIO uses bus identifier KVM_PIO_BUS.

Encrypted-state MSR intercept policy leaves hardware-switched registers uninterrupted, including the GHCB, EFER and PAT registers. TSC auxiliary interception follows RDTSCP and RDPID guest capability when the virtual TSC auxiliary feature exists. Guest TSC frequency read interception is suppressed only while secure TSC is active. XSS interception follows whether XSAVES is both usable and exposed to the guest.
Disabling an MSR intercept is expressed as setting the intercept state to false for the given register and access type. It is a thin convenience over the general intercept setter.

After CPUID is set for an SEV guest, the reserved GPA mask is relaxed for the encryption position derived from leaf 8000001F. The low bits of EBX in that leaf select which physical address bit becomes non-reserved. Absence of the leaf leaves the mask unchanged.

Preparation for entry to an encrypted-state guest preserves host state that hardware reloads or resets but does not save. Extended control state, protection key rights and supervisor state are captured. Debug address masks are captured when debug swapping is possible, including a conservative SNP case, while actual debug registers remain under common restore logic. TSC auxiliary is captured from the user-return slot when virtualized.

StartupIPI vector delivery distinguishes the first wake from later wakes. The first wake only records arrival and preserves values established by the VMM. Later wakes complete a pending AP reset hold according to the negotiated mechanism, either by completing a non-auto-exit event with nonzero status or by writing result and response fields into the GHCB info word. Unknown hold types perform no action.

SNP-safe page allocation yields a zeroed single page whose frame is not 2M aligned when running on an SNP-capable host. It does so by allocating two contiguous pages, splitting them, keeping the unaligned member and freeing its buddy. On hosts without SNP support it is equivalent to a normal zeroed node allocation.

On SNP hosts certain control pages must avoid 2M alignment or the CPU may raise a spurious RMP fault when a huge page collides with their RMP entry. The allocator invariant above exists to avoid that erratum for VMCB, VMSA and AVIC backing pages.

A frame range is considered shared only when every RMP entry lookup succeeds and reports unassigned. Any lookup error or any assigned entry causes the whole range to be treated as not shared. A 2M RMP update is considered possible only for a large folio whose entire enclosing 2M aligned window satisfies that shared test.

Conversion of guest memory to private is a no-op for non-SNP VMs and accepts only single-page requests. It first consults the RMP entry and treats already-assigned frames as success. Otherwise it selects 2M granularity when the enclosing window allows a large RMP update and 4K otherwise, then records the frame as private with the VM address space identifier.

Conversion of guest memory to shared walks each frame in the range and skips frames whose lookup fails or that are already unassigned. Aligned runs covered by a large RMP entry convert with one 2M update. A large entry touched by an unaligned request is first split into 4K entries. Each converted frame is flushed from caches with a width matching its conversion granularity, and the walk yields periodically.

Invalidation of guest memory ranges requires the VM address-space lock held for write. While holding it the routine may read each VCPU guest VMSA address without that VCPU lock. That read can yield false positives but not false negatives because the address can only become valid under the same write lock, so a spurious kick is benign.

Range invalidation affects only SNP VMs. Every VCPU whose recorded guest VMSA address is valid and falls inside the invalidated guest frame interval receives a VMSA reload request and kick, forcing it to re-establish its VMSA mapping.

If a kernel PIO device disappears after part of a multi-element transfer has completed, the remainder is not redirected to userspace. Output remainders are dropped and input remainders are zero filled, after which the partial transfer reports kernel-handled status.

SNP debug decrypt always returns its target page to hypervisor ownership. If that return fails the page is leaked and never used, even when the decrypt itself succeeded. Firmware command failures are logged with return and firmware error codes and release the scratch page. Shared conversion logs but tolerates split failures and still attempts the sharing update.

Intercept policy references architectural registers GHCB, EFER, PAT, TSC_AUX, guest TSC frequency and XSS, plus CPU features RDTSCP, RDPID, XSAVES and virtual TSC auxiliary. CPUID leaf 8000001F EBX low bits encode the SEV physical address reduction position.
